{{Short description|Endofunctor on the category of simplicial sets}}
{{Other uses|Extension (disambiguation)}}In [[higher category theory]] in [[mathematics]], the '''extension''' of [[Simplicial set|simplicial sets]] ('''extension functor''' or '''Ex functor''') is an [[endofunctor]] on the [[category of simplicial sets]]. Due to many remarkable properties, the extension functor has plenty and strong applications in homotopical algebra. Among the most well-known is its application in the construction of [[Kan complexes]] from arbitrary simplicial sets, which often enables [[without loss of generality]] to take the former for proofs about the latter. It is furthermore very well compatible with the [[Kan–Quillen model structure]] and can for example be used to explicitly state its factorizations or to search for [[Weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak homotopy equivalences]].

== Definition ==
Using the [[Subdivision (simplicial set)|subdivision]] of simplicial sets, the extension of simplicial sets is defined as:<ref>Cisinski 2019, p. 81</ref><ref name=":2">Guillou, Definition 6</ref>

: <math>
\operatorname{Ex}\colon
\mathbf{sSet}\rightarrow\mathbf{sSet},
\operatorname{Ex}(Y)_n
:=\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^n),Y).
</math>

Due to the [[Yoneda lemma]], one also has <math>\operatorname{Ex}(Y)_n
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta^n,\operatorname{Ex}(Y))
</math>.<ref name=":2" /> All connecting maps of the sets are given by precomposition with the application of the subdivision functor to all canonical inclusions <math>\Delta^{n-1}\hookrightarrow\Delta^n</math>. Since the subdivision functor by definition commutes with all [[colimits]], and for every simplicial set <math>X</math> there is an [[isomorphism]]:<ref>Guillou, Proposition 1</ref>

: <math>X\cong\varinjlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\Delta^n,</math>

it is in fact [[left adjoint]] to the extension functor, denoted <math>\operatorname{Sd}\dashv\operatorname{Ex}</math>.<ref name=":2" /> For simplicial sets <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>, one has:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sd}(X),Y)
&\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sd}(\varinjlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\Delta^n),Y)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\varinjlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^n),Y)
\cong\varprojlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^n),Y) \\
&\cong\varprojlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\operatorname{Hom}(\Delta^n,\operatorname{Ex}(Y))
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(\varinjlim_{\Delta^n\rightarrow X}\Delta^n,\operatorname{Ex}(Y))
\cong\operatorname{Hom}(X,\operatorname{Ex}(Y)).
\end{align}
</math>

It is therefore possible to also simply define the extension functor as the right adjoint to the subdivision functor. Both of their construction as extension by colimits and definition is similar to that of the adjunction between [[Geometric realization functor|geometric realization]] and the singular functor, with an important difference being that there is '''no''' isomorphism:

: <math>X\cong\varinjlim_{|\Delta^n|\rightarrow X}|\Delta^n|</math>

for every topological space <math>X</math>. This is because the colimit is always a [[CW complex]], for which the isomorphism does indeed hold.

The [[natural transformation]] <math>a\colon\operatorname{Sd}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Id}</math> induces a natural transformation <math>b\colon
\operatorname{Id}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}</math> under the adjunction <math>\operatorname{Sd}\dashv\operatorname{Ex}</math>. In particular there is a canonical morphism <math>b_X\colon
X\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}(X)</math> for every simplicial set <math>X</math>.

== Ex∞ functor ==
For a simplicial set <math>X</math>, the canonical morphism <math>b_X\colon
X\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}(X)</math> includes an <math>\mathbb{N}</math>-shaped [[Cone (category theory)|cone]] <math>X\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}(X)\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^2(X)\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^3(X)\rightarrow\ldots</math>, whose [[Limit (category theory)|limit]] is denoted:<ref>Cisinski 2019,  Equation (3.1.22.4)</ref><ref>Guillou, Definition 7</ref>

: <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)
:=\varinjlim_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname{Ex}^n(X).
</math>

Since limit and colimit are switched, there is '''no''' adjunction <math>\operatorname{Sd}^\infty\dashv\operatorname{Ex}^\infty</math> with the [[Sd∞ functor]]. But for the study of simplices, this is of no concern as any <math>m</math>-simplex <math>\Delta^m\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)</math> due to the [[compactness]] of the standard <math>m</math>-simplex <math>\Delta^m</math> factors over a morphism <math>\Delta^m\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^n(X)</math> for a <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>, for which the adjunction <math>\operatorname{Sd}^n\dashv\operatorname{Ex}^n</math> can then be applied to get a morphism <math>\operatorname{Sd}^n(\Delta^m)\rightarrow X</math>.

The natural transformation <math>b\colon
\operatorname{Id}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}</math> induces a natural transformation <math>\beta\colon
\operatorname{Id}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^\infty</math>. In particular there is a canonical morphism <math>\beta_X\colon
X\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)</math> for every simplicial set <math>X</math>.

== Properties ==

* For every simplicial set <math>X</math>, the canonical morphism <math>b_X\colon
X\rightarrow\operatorname{Ex}(X)</math> is a [[Weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak homotopy equivalence]].<ref>Goerss & Jardine 1999, Theorem 4.6.</ref><ref>Cisinski 2019, Proposition 3.1.21</ref>
* The extension functor <math>
\operatorname{Ex}
</math> preserves weak homotopy equivalences (which follows directly from the preceding property and their 2-of-3 property) and [[Kan fibration|Kan fibrations]],<ref>Goerss & Jardine 1999, Lemma 4.5. for Kan fibrations for Ex</ref> hence fibrations and trivial fibrations of the [[Kan–Quillen model structure]]. This makes the adjunction <math>\operatorname{Sd}\dashv\operatorname{Ex}</math> even into a [[Quillen adjunction]] <math>\operatorname{Sd}\colon
\mathbf{sSet}_\mathrm{KQ}\rightleftarrows\mathbf{sSet}_\mathrm{KQ}\colon
\operatorname{Ex}</math>.
* For every horn inclusion <math>\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Ex}(X)</math> with a simplicial set <math>X</math> there exists an extension <math>\Delta^n\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^2(X)</math>.<ref>Goerss & Jardine 1999, Lemma 4.7.</ref><ref>Guillou, Lemma 1</ref>
* For every simplicial set <math>X</math>, the simplicial set <math>\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)</math> is a [[Kan complex]], hence a fibrant object of the Kan–Quillen model structure.<ref name=":3">Goerss & Jardine 1999, Theorem 4.8. on p. 188</ref><ref>Cisinski 2019, Theorem 3.1.27</ref><ref name=":4">Guillou, Properties of Ex∞</ref> This follows directly from the preceding property. Furthermore the canonical morphism <math>\beta_X\colon
X\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)</math> is a [[monomorphism]] and a [[Weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak homotopy equivalence]], hence a trivial cofibration of the Kan–Quillen model structure.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /> <math>\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)</math> is therefore the ''fibrant replacement'' of <math>X</math> in the Kan–Quillen model structure, hence the [[factorization]] of the [[Terminal object|terminal]] morphism <math>X\rightarrow\Delta^0</math> in a trivial cofibration followed by a fibration. Furthermore, there is a restriction <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty\colon
\mathbf{sSet}\rightarrow\mathbf{Kan}
</math> with the [[subcategory]] <math>
\mathbf{Kan}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{sSet}
</math> of Kan complexes.
* The infinite extension functor <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty
</math> preserves all three classes of the Kan–Quillen model structure, hence Kan fibrations, monomorphisms and weak homotopy equivalences (which again follows directly from the preceding property and their 2-of-3 property).<ref>Cisinski 2019, Proposition 3.1.23.</ref><ref>Goerss & Jardine 1999, Theorem 4.8. (3) for Kan fibrations for Ex∞</ref>
* The extension functor <math>
\operatorname{Ex}
</math> and the infinite extension functor <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty
</math> both preserve the set of <math>0</math>-simplices, which follows directly from <math>
\operatorname{Sd}(\Delta^0)
\cong\Delta^0
</math>. For a simplicial set <math>X</math>, one has:<ref>Cisinski 2019, 3.8.6.</ref>
*:<math>
\operatorname{Ex}(X)_0
=X_0,
</math>
*: <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty(X)_0
=X_0.
</math>
* The extension functor fixes the singular functor. For a [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, one has:

:: <math>
\operatorname{Ex}\operatorname{Sing}(X)
\cong\operatorname{Sing}(X).
</math>
: This follows from <math>
|\operatorname{Sd}(X)|
\cong|X|
</math> for every simplicial set <math>X</math><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Lurie |first=Jacob |author-link=Jacob Lurie |title=Kerodon, Proposition 3.3.3.7. |url=https://kerodon.net/tag/00YB |access-date=2025-04-19 |website=kerodon.net |language=en}}</ref> by using the adjunctions <math>|-|\dashv\operatorname{Sing}</math> and <math>\operatorname{Sd}\dashv\operatorname{Ex}</math>. In particular, for a topological space <math>X</math>, one has:
:: <math>
\operatorname{Ex}^\infty\operatorname{Sing}(X)
\cong\operatorname{Sing}(X),
</math>
: which fits the fact that the singular functor already produces a Kan complex, which can be its own fibrant replacement.
